Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong
keep mind occupied all the time

issues.item: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: This item is not clearly coherent with the rest of the profile. The other Threat items describe re-experiencing and hypervigilance after sudden movements, but risky behavior reflects disinhibition/behavioral dyscontrol rather than a trauma-linked threat response. It can occur in PTSD, but in this formulation it sits somewhat apart from the other selected threat items.

issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: This is clinically plausible for a sexual assault survivor, but it creates a very specific external-trigger threat pattern. Because all trigger→threat edges are inactive, this item should not imply a strongly cue-linked chain that is otherwise absent. It is still usable, but only as a mild issue in coherence with the formulation.

vignette:
Hassan, a 52-year-old Middle Eastern network engineer in a long-term relationship, came to treatment describing how a sexual assault that occurred several months earlier had left him feeling as though his body never fully returned to the present. The assault happened after work one evening, when he had stayed late to resolve a network outage at a client site and was caught off guard by someone he knew socially but did not trust well. In the weeks that followed, certain moments began to pull him back into the scene with unsettling force. If someone stood too close in a hallway, if a hand brushed his shoulder unexpectedly, or if he was alone in a dim office while troubleshooting a system, he would suddenly feel as if the event were happening again; his chest tightened, his stomach dropped, and he found himself scanning the room as though he needed to get away immediately. The memories were not distant recollections for him but abrupt intrusions that arrived with a rush of fear, disgust, and shame.

Hassan said the worst part was how quickly his mind turned against him afterward. He kept circling over what he should have noticed, what he should have said, and why he had not prevented it. He had come to believe that some mistake in his own judgment had opened the door to what happened, and he spent long stretches replaying the evening in his head, searching for the moment he might have done something differently. That self-blame did not stay in his thoughts alone; it shaped how he moved through daily life. The more vividly the memories and bodily reactions hit him, the more he tried to keep his mind occupied all the time, filling every quiet moment with work emails, technical podcasts, news, or endlessly checking devices so there would be no room for the images. He also began avoiding other people, not only strangers but colleagues after hours and social gatherings with friends, because being around others made him feel exposed and vulnerable in ways he could not easily explain.

Over time, Hassan's avoidance narrowed his world. At his job as a network engineer, where he spent much of the day in server rooms, on conference calls, and moving between different office floors, he became increasingly tense when he had to enter unfamiliar spaces or work late with only one other person present. He started volunteering for tasks that let him remain alone at his desk and declined invitations to team dinners. He told himself that staying busy kept him functional, but he also knew that any lull gave the memories room to break through. When they did, the physical jolt was immediate enough that he would grip the edge of his chair or step into a restroom to steady himself. The more often this happened, the more certain he became that something inside him was permanently damaged, and the more carefully he watched for signs that another reminder was near. That constant alertness made him even more withdrawn, as if staying out of people's way might keep the assault from finding him again.

His partner had noticed how much he had changed. Hassan was still living at home and trying to maintain the routines of work, but he had grown quieter, less present, and increasingly exhausted by the effort of forcing himself through each day. The strain became harder to hide when a routine issue at work placed him in a cramped equipment room with another technician; the sudden closeness and the smell of the enclosed space triggered a wave of fear so intense that he had to leave before the problem was finished. He later spent hours alone, replaying the incident and blaming himself for not handling it better, which only deepened his urge to keep busy and stay away from people. By the time he sought help, his PCL-5 score reflected what he already felt in his daily life: that the assault was still intruding into the present, and that his efforts to outrun it were steadily shrinking the life he and his partner had built. What finally brought him in was the fear that he would not be able to keep working this way much longer, and his hope that treatment might help him stay in the room without feeling as though the assault was happening all over again.
